title: An automated blood test for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin carboxy-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) to predict the absence of intracranial lesions on head CT in adult patients with mild traumatic brain injury: BRAINI, a multicentre observational study in Europe
article_subtype: Prospective, multicentre observational diagnostic accuracy study
condition_or_topic: Use of blood biomarkers to exclude intracranial lesions on head CT after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI).
clinical_background: Head CT is the reference method for identifying intracranial lesions during acute assessment of mTBI, although most patients do not develop intracranial complications. Clinical decision rules help guide CT use, but prescribing practices vary. S100B protein has been incorporated into some European guidance for selected patients, while GFAP and UCH-L1 have been proposed as biomarkers with a longer post-injury testing window. In the ALERT-TBI study, their combined test showed high sensitivity and negative predictive value, but its cutoffs had not been externally validated using a rapid automated assay suitable for emergency care. The relationship between biomarker concentrations at injury and later neurological outcome also required further study.
objectives: Primarily, externally validate the predetermined GFAP and UCH-L1 cutoffs using an automated immunoassay in a European multicentre cohort, estimating the sensitivity and negative predictive value of the combined test for excluding intracranial lesions on head CT after mTBI.
Compare the diagnostic performance of GFAP and UCH-L1 with S100B protein.
Compare the combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test with commonly used clinical decision rules assigned retrospectively, to assess whether biomarkers might inform decisions about head CT.
Assess neurological deterioration at 7 days and outcome at 3 months in relation to biomarker results as potential prognostic indicators.
clinical_question: In patients with mTBI undergoing head CT, how accurately does an automated blood test combining GFAP and UCH-L1 at predetermined cutoffs exclude CT-detected intracranial lesions, particularly in terms of sensitivity and negative predictive value? Secondary comparisons concern S100B protein and retrospectively assigned clinical decision rules, alongside neurological outcomes at 7 days and 3 months.
study_design: BRAINI was a prospective, multicentre observational study conducted at 16 emergency departments in France and Spain. Recruitment took place between August 2019 and June 2021. Biomarker measurements were performed without access to clinical or CT findings, and head CT scans were assessed centrally by independent neuroradiologists unaware of clinical and biomarker results. CT prescribing was independent of biomarker results.

population.description: Patients presenting after mild traumatic brain injury with an admission GCS score of 13–15 who underwent routine head CT and provided a blood sample within 12 h of injury. Of 1508 patients assessed for eligibility, 1438 had biomarker results and a valid head CT scan for the main analysis. Median age was 69 years (IQR 44–83).
inclusion_criteria: Age ≥18 years in France or ≥15 years in Spain.
GCS score of 13–15 after traumatic brain injury, with altered brain function or other evidence of brain pathology caused by an external force.
Routine head CT scan and blood sampling within 12 h after injury.
exclusion_criteria: Unknown injury time, or unknown timing of CT or blood sampling, or either procedure occurring more than 12 h after injury.
Admission for a non-traumatic neurological disorder or a penetrating head injury.

Dementia, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, seizure disorder, brain tumor, prior neurosurgery, stroke within the last 30 days, or major psychiatric disease that could interfere with outcome assessment.
Venipuncture not feasible or head CT not performed.
Subject under judiciary control, pregnancy or breastfeeding, or participation in an ongoing interventional trial.
population.care_setting: Emergency departments at 16 sites in France and Spain, comprising trauma centres and community hospitals.

interventions: Diagnostic testing of a 10-ml blood sample for serum GFAP and UCH-L1 using automated VIDAS® 3 platform immunoassays. The combined test was positive if either concentration was at or above its predefined cutoff of 22 pg/ml for GFAP or 327 pg/ml for UCH-L1; it was negative if both were below their cutoffs.
Serum S100B protein testing in a consenting subset with sufficient samples, using Elecsys® S100 on the automated Cobas® system and a cutoff of 0.1 μg/L.
comparators: Head CT, centrally classified as positive or negative for traumatic intracranial lesions, served as the diagnostic reference.
The diagnostic performance of the combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test was compared with GFAP alone, UCH-L1 alone and, in the subset with results available, S100B protein.
The combined test was compared with retrospectively assigned, adapted Canadian CT Head Injury Rule (a-CCHR) and New Orleans Criteria (a-NOC).

primary: Sensitivity and negative predictive value (NPV) of the combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test for ruling out intracranial lesions on head CT.
secondary: Specificity and positive predictive value (PPV) of the combined test, and diagnostic performance of GFAP, UCH-L1 and S100B protein individually.
Diagnostic performance of the combined test relative to a-CCHR and a-NOC.
Neurological worsening at 7 days, defined as a GCS decrease of greater than 2 points from baseline or deterioration requiring osmotherapy, intensive care transfer or neurosurgical intervention.
Neurological outcome at 3 months assessed with GOSE and RPQ. Incomplete recovery was defined as GOSE <8; persistent symptoms related to PCS were classified using the stated RPQ symptom criteria.

statistical_methods: The sample-size calculation sought sensitivity of 98% significantly above 93%, with a 2.5% type I error and 80% power; it required at least 173 CT-positive patients. Assuming 11% CT positivity gave 1573 patients, rounded to 1600, and a further 10% allowance for screening failures set a recruitment target of 1760. Quantitative variables were summarized by median and quartiles, and categorical variables by counts and percentages. CT-positive and CT-negative groups were compared using Mann–Whitney U, Chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests as appropriate. Outcomes were analysed using complete available data without imputation. Prespecified analyses examined age and sex; sensitivity analyses examined GCS score and time from injury to blood sampling. ROC areas and 95% confidence intervals were estimated, with biomarker ROC areas compared using the DeLong algorithm. Sensitivity, specificity, NPV and PPV received 95% confidence intervals calculated by the Agresti-Coull method. Comparisons with a-CCHR and a-NOC used McNemar tests for sensitivity and specificity and the Leisenring generalized score statistic for NPV and PPV. Biomarker concentrations by neurological outcome were compared with Mann–Whitney U tests; multivariate logistic regression adjusted associations for age, sex and admission GCS score. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05, and analyses used Stata version 17.0.
follow_up: Neurological worsening was assessed at 7 days, and GOSE and RPQ outcomes were assessed at 3 months after injury.
interpretation: Using the predetermined GFAP and UCH-L1 cutoffs, the automated combined test showed high sensitivity and negative predictive value for excluding CT-detectable intracranial lesions after mTBI. Its diagnostic performance was maintained with blood sampling up to 12 h after injury. GFAP alone had the highest sensitivity and negative predictive value; this study did not confirm an additional diagnostic benefit from UCH-L1. Specificity declined with age, particularly among patients aged 80 and over. Higher biomarker concentrations at admission were associated with poorer neurological outcomes at 3 months, but the differences were small and their prognostic value remains uncertain.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The findings externally validate cutoffs established in the ALERT-TBI study using an automated assay that provides results in less than 1 h, rather than the earlier manual method requiring 4 h. Unlike ALERT-TBI, this study did not confirm that adding UCH-L1 improves the diagnostic performance of GFAP; the authors suggest that differences in patient age or time to sampling might explain this. The combined test performed better than S100B when sampling occurred beyond 3 h after injury, consistent with other studies cited by the authors. Reduced specificity in older patients was also consistent with previous reports. Comparisons suggesting an advantage over CCHR and NOC remain tentative because those rules were adapted and applied retrospectively.
clinical_implications: The combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test could help identify adults with mTBI who do not have CT-detectable intracranial lesions and thereby reduce unnecessary head CT scans.
Results available in less than 1 h and diagnostic performance maintained over a 12 h post-injury sampling window could make the test useful in emergency care.
Lower specificity in older patients means fewer negative tests in that population; the authors suggest that its cutoffs should be reconsidered for older adults.
Admission biomarker concentrations may contribute to future models of incomplete recovery, but the small observed differences require confirmation before a prognostic role can be established.
practice_implications: The authors report that recent French National Recommendations suggest S100B testing within the first 3 h after injury or the combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test within 12 h after injury, if available.
The authors do not establish a clinical algorithm for using biomarker results to decide whether to order CT: in this validation study, CT was prescribed independently of those results.
limitations: BRAINI was a validation study, not an implementation study; it did not test biomarker-guided CT decisions in routine care.
Indications for CT differed across countries, centres and attending physicians.
The proportion of CT-positive patients was higher than expected, although the observed negative predictive value met the prespecified expectations.
Alternative biomarker cutoffs were not assessed.

The comparisons with clinical decision rules used adapted versions applied retrospectively to recorded risk factors rather than physicians’ prospective assessments; this may have affected their performance.
The study was neither designed nor powered to formally assess comparisons with clinical decision rules, neurological deterioration at 7 days, or outcomes at 3 months.
The cohort was relatively old and falls were the predominant injury mechanism, which may limit generalisability to younger emergency-department populations with different injury mechanisms.
Although biomarker concentrations differed significantly by neurological status at 3 months, the differences were small and warrant caution.
The investigators could not determine the total number of potentially screened patients.
strengths: The authors describe the study as, to their knowledge, the largest direct comparison of two brain-biomarker approaches available for clinical use in Europe.
The study externally validated predetermined cutoffs in a multicentre European cohort using an automated assay designed to deliver results in less than 1 h.
open_questions: Whether UCH-L1 adds diagnostic value to GFAP alone, particularly in populations differing in age or time from injury to blood sampling.
How accurately the biomarkers perform outside traumatic injury, including intracerebral haematoma and subarachnoid haemorrhage.
How blood biomarkers and clinical decision rules should be combined in an algorithm for CT decisions, and how that approach performs in routine care.
Whether the modest associations between admission biomarker concentrations and later symptoms or incomplete recovery can support useful prognostic models.
future_directions: Evaluate biomarker-guided CT triage in real-world implementation studies.
Optimise biomarker cutoffs for older adults and paediatric patients.
Develop and assess an algorithm combining clinical factors with blood biomarkers.
Investigate biomarker performance in non-traumatic intracranial conditions.
Confirm the associations between biomarker concentrations and neurological outcomes before developing models to identify patients at risk of incomplete recovery after mTBI.

main_findings.description: The combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test identified patients with CT-detected intracranial lesions with high sensitivity.
main_findings.context: The primary analysis included 1438 patients; the combined test was positive in 176 of the CT-positive patients and negative in 3.

main_findings.description: A negative combined GFAP–UCH-L1 result strongly predicted the absence of intracranial lesions on head CT.
main_findings.n_events: 314 CT-negative patients among 317 with a negative test
main_findings.context: This was a primary outcome in the 1438-patient analysis.

main_findings.description: The combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test had limited specificity for CT-detected intracranial lesions.
main_findings.n_events: 314 CT-negative patients with a negative test
main_findings.context: The primary analysis included 1259 CT-negative patients.

main_findings.description: The combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test had the reported positive predictive value for intracranial lesions on CT.
main_findings.n_events: 176 CT-positive patients among 1121 with a positive test

main_findings.description: Three patients had intracranial findings on CT despite a negative combined biomarker result. Two had subarachnoid haemorrhage following rupture of a non-traumatic intracranial aneurysm; the third had a barely visible subarachnoid haemorrhage without subsequent neurological deterioration.
main_findings.context: The authors state that all 3 would have undergone CT under CCHR criteria.

subgroup_analyses: Among patients aged ≥65 years, combined-test specificity was 10.3% (95% CI 8.2–12.8), compared with 42.1% (95% CI 38.1–46.1) in younger patients (p < 0.001). Specificity was 6.0% at age 80 and over. Negative combined-test results occurred in 38% of patients below 65 years versus 8% of older patients.

Patient sex, a GCS score of 15, and injury-to-sampling intervals of <3 h, 3–6 h, or >6 h did not affect combined-test performance. The authors report that its diagnostic performance persisted across the 12 h sampling window.

During the first 3 h after trauma, S100B protein had the same sensitivity and negative predictive value as the combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test; beyond 3 h, both measures were lower for S100B protein. Among 98 patients sampled within the first 2 h, the biomarkers did not differ in diagnostic performance.

In the subset with concomitant S100B protein results, the diagnostic findings were unchanged in patients with isolated TBI (n = 258 patients) and those with multiple extra-cranial injuries (n = 82 patients).
secondary_results: Of 1508 patients assessed between August 2019 and June 2021, 40 did not meet inclusion criteria, blood samples were unavailable for 27, and CT results were unavailable for three. The analysis comprised 1438 patients. Median age was 69 years (IQR 44–83); 179 (12.4%) had a traumatic intracranial lesion on CT, while 1259 were CT-negative.

CT positivity did not differ significantly between France and Spain: 11.1 vs 14.3%, respectively (p = 0.07). For the first two central CT readers, positive specific agreement was 85%, negative specific agreement was 98%, and the kappa coefficient was 0.83.

Reported intracranial lesions included subarachnoid haemorrhage in 104 patients (58%), acute subdural haematomas in 77 (43%), intraparenchymal contusions in 36 (20%), epidural haematoma in 26 (14.5%), petechial haemorrhage in 10 (5.6%), and intraventricular haemorrhage in 9 (5%).

In the full population, 1121 patients (78%) had a positive combined GFAP–UCH-L1 result and 317 (22%) had a negative result. The CT-positive and CT-negative counts, respectively, were 176 and 945 among test-positive patients, and 3 and 314 among test-negative patients.

For GFAP alone in the study population, CT-positive and CT-negative denominators were N = 178 and N = 1258. Sensitivity was 98.3 (95% CI 94.9–99.7), specificity 31.3 (95% CI 28.8–33.9), NPV 99.2 (95% CI 97.7–99.9), and PPV 16.8 (95% CI 14.7–19.2); these measures are percentages. Among Test+ (N = 1039), 175 were CT-positive and 864 CT-negative; among Test− (N = 397), 3 were CT-positive and 394 CT-negative.

For UCH-L1 alone in the study population, CT-positive and CT-negative denominators were N = 179 and N = 1258. Sensitivity was 57.0 (95% CI 49.7–64.0), specificity 63.0 (95% CI 60.3–65.7), NPV 91.1 (95% CI 89.1–92.9), and PPV 18.0 (95% CI 15.0–21.4); these measures are percentages. Among Test+ (N = 567), 102 were CT-positive and 465 CT-negative; among Test− (N = 870), 77 were CT-positive and 793 CT-negative.

Among 1210 patients with concomitant S100B protein analysis, 761 had a positive S100B protein test and 937 had a positive combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test. For S100B protein, the CT-positive and CT-negative denominators were N = 153 and N = 1057. Sensitivity was 83.0 (95% CI 76.2–88.2), specificity 40.0 (95% CI 37.1–43.0), NPV 94.2 (95% CI 91.6–96.0), and PPV 16.7 (95% CI 14.2–19.5); these measures are percentages. Among Test+ (N = 761), 127 were CT-positive and 634 CT-negative; among Test− (N = 449), 26 were CT-positive and 423 CT-negative.

Within the 1210-patient S100B protein subset, the combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test had sensitivity 98.7 (95% CI 95.1–99.9), specificity 25.6 (95% CI 23.1–28.4), NPV 99.3 (95% CI 97.2–100), and PPV 16.1 (95% CI 14.9–19.9); these measures are percentages. The CT-positive and CT-negative denominators were N = 153 and N = 1057. Among Test+ (N = 937), 151 were CT-positive and 786 CT-negative; among Test− (N = 273), 2 were CT-positive and 271 CT-negative.

Within the S100B protein subset, GFAP alone had sensitivity 98.7 (95% CI 95.0–99.9), specificity 31.8 (95% CI 29.1–34.7), NPV 99.4 (95% CI 97.7–100), and PPV 17.2 (95% CI 14.9–19.9); these measures are percentages. The CT-positive and CT-negative denominators were N = 152 and N = 1056. Among Test+ (N = 870), 150 were CT-positive and 720 CT-negative; among Test− (N = 338), 2 were CT-positive and 336 CT-negative.

Within the S100B protein subset, UCH-L1 alone had sensitivity 55.6 (95% CI 47.6–63.6), specificity 65.4 (95% CI 62.5–68.2), NPV 91.0 (95% CI 88.8–92.9), and PPV 18.9 (95% CI 15.5–22.8); these measures are percentages. The CT-positive and CT-negative denominators were N = 153 and N = 1056. Among Test+ (N = 450), 85 were CT-positive and 365 CT-negative; among Test− (N = 759), 68 were CT-positive and 691 CT-negative.

GFAP and UCH-L1 concentrations were significantly higher in CT-positive than CT-negative patients: GFAP, 182.9 [71.8–320.0] versus 35.2 [17.6–65.7] pg/ml (p <0.0001); UCH-L1, 360 [221–608] versus 265 [166–462] pg/ml (p <0.0001). For detection of CT lesions in the full analysis, GFAP had a greater area under the curve than UCH-L1: 0.85 (95% CI 0.82–0.88) versus 0.63 (95% CI 0.58–0.67), p < 0.001. In the S100B protein subset, the corresponding areas were 0.85 (95% CI 0.82–0.88) for GFAP, 0.64 (95% CI 0.59–0.68) for UCH-L1, and 0.66 (95% CI 0.62–0.71) for S100B protein; GFAP was higher than the other biomarkers (p < 0.001).

The retrospectively assigned, adapted rules a-CCHR and a-NOC had lower NPV and specificity than the combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test. Under a-CCHR, 1199 patients (83% of the sample) would have been classified as requiring CT; among the remaining 239 (17%), 10 had CT-detectable intracranial lesions and a positive combined biomarker test. Considered independently of CCHR, the combined test could have avoided 317 (22%) unnecessary CT scans but would have missed CT abnormalities in 3 patients. The rule comparison was based on retrospectively adapted criteria.

Neurological worsening occurred in 11 patients at 7 days; all deterioration was TBI-related, and none required ICU admission or neurosurgical intervention. GFAP was higher in those with worsening than in those without it: 320 pg/ml (Q1–Q3 42.5–630) versus 39.8 pg/ml (Q1–Q3 20.0–80.5), p = 0.004. No statistically significant association with worsening was shown for S100B or UCH-L1.

At 3 months, GOSE data were available for 1062 (74%) patients and RPQ data for 1012 (70%). Incomplete recovery, defined by GOSE <8, occurred in 269 patients (25.3%); PCS-related symptoms according to RPQ occurred in 246 (24.3%).

For GOSE <8 (N = 269) versus GOSE 8 (N = 793) at 3 months, admission median [25–75th percentiles] concentrations were GFAP 54.9 [27.9–145] versus 39.0 [18.2–77.6] pg/ml (p <0.001; age-, sex-, and admission-GCS-adjusted p <0.001); UCH-L1 327 [194–552] versus 248 [160–412] pg/ml (p <0.001; adjusted p <0.001); and S100B protein 0.18 [0.09–0.32] versus 0.12 [0.07–0.20] μg/ml (p <0.001; adjusted p <0.001).

For post-concussion symptoms (N = 246) versus no post-concussion symptoms (N = 766) at 3 months, admission median [25–75th percentiles] concentrations were GFAP 47.4 [27.0–84.6] versus 39.3 [18.7–84.6] pg/mL (p = 0.01; adjusted p = 0.004); UCH-L1 280 [181–511] versus 260 [162–431] pg/ml (p = 0.024; adjusted p = 0.001); and S100B protein 0.16 [0.08–0.28] versus 0.12 [0.07–0.21] μg/ml (p = 0.003; adjusted p = 0.18). The adjusted S100B protein result was not statistically significant.

The reported areas under the curve for incomplete recovery were 0.61 for GFAP, 0.60 for UCH-L-1, and 0.61 for S100B; for persistent PCS symptoms, they were 0.56, 0.55, and 0.57, respectively. The authors reported greater prognostic sensitivity for GFAP and the combined GFAP-UCH-L1 test, while describing the biomarker concentration differences associated with later outcomes as small.

tables.summary: Patients with CT-detected injury were older and had higher ISS scores and admission concentrations of GFAP and UCH-L1. They more often received antiplatelet agents and had GCS scores of 13 or 14. Continuous values are medians [25–75th percentiles] unless otherwise indicated.

tables.summary: The combined test had high sensitivity and NPV but low specificity in the full study population. The S100B subset permits comparison of all four tests. Performance estimates are percentages followed by 95% confidence intervals; CT classifications and test counts are displayed separately for each biomarker.

tables.title: Admission biomarker concentrations by neurological outcome at 3 months
tables.summary: Admission biomarker concentrations were generally higher among patients with incomplete recovery or post-concussion symptoms at 3 months. Adjusted p-values come from logistic regression accounting for age, sex and admission GCS; the adjusted association between S100B protein and post-concussion symptoms was not statistically significant. Concentrations are medians [25–75th percentiles].

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that automated GFAP–UCH-L1 testing with the evaluated cutoffs could support accurate, rapid screening of patients with mTBI for the absence of CT-detectable intracranial injury. They suggest that the combination may discriminate better than S100B protein when blood is drawn beyond 3 h after trauma.
narrative_summary: BRAINI prospectively evaluated an automated blood test in patients with mTBI at 16 emergency departments in France and Spain. Participants underwent head CT and provided blood within 12 h of injury; the analysis included 1438 patients, of whom 179 (12.4%) had an intracranial lesion on CT. The combined test classified a result as negative only when GFAP was below 22 pg/ml and UCH-L1 was below 327 pg/ml. It had sensitivity of 98.3% (95% CI 95.0–99.7), NPV of 99.1% (95% CI 97.1–99.8) and specificity of 24.9% (95% CI 22.6–27.4). Among 317 patients with negative combined results, 3 had positive CT scans; two had subarachnoid haemorrhage associated with a non-traumatic ruptured aneurysm, and the third had a minimal subarachnoid haemorrhage without subsequent neurological deterioration. In the subset tested for S100B protein, the combined test performed better for sensitivity and NPV beyond 3 h after injury. Specificity declined with older age. Higher admission biomarker concentrations were associated with incomplete recovery or persistent symptoms at 3 months, although differences were small and the study was not designed or powered to formally assess prognosis. The authors consider the assay potentially useful for rapid CT triage, while noting that CT decisions were independent of test results and that its use in a clinical decision algorithm still requires evaluation.

document_sections.heading: Summary
document_sections.content: The summary presents the rationale, design, diagnostic findings and interpretation of BRAINI. Its component sections provide the details.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Raised blood concentrations of GFAP and UCH-L1 after mTBI may indicate lesions detectable on head CT. The investigators sought to validate whether their combination, measured by an automated immunoassay at predetermined cutoffs, could identify patients without intracranial lesions.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: This prospective observational study involved 16 emergency departments in France and Spain. Eligible adults with mTBI underwent head CT and supplied a 10-ml blood sample within 12 h of injury. Serum GFAP and UCH-L1 were assessed in less than an hour against respective cutoffs of 22 pg/ml and 327 pg/ml. S100B protein was also measured in a subset. The primary measures were sensitivity and NPV of the combined test for excluding lesions on head CT. The study was registered as ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04032509.

document_sections.heading: Findings
document_sections.content: Between August 2019 and June 2021, 1508 patients were recruited and 1438 entered the main analysis. Median age was 69 years (IQR 44–83), and most patients (74%) presented 3 h after trauma. CT identified intracranial lesions in 179 (12.4%) patients. Combined-test sensitivity was 98.3% (95% CI 95.0–99.7), specificity was 24.9 (95% CI 22.6–27.4), and NPV was 99.1% (95% CI 97.1–99.8). Three patients with positive CT findings tested negative for the biomarkers. S100B sensitivity was 83.0% (95% CI 76.2–88.2), with an NPV of 94.2% (95% CI 91.6–96.0). Higher biomarker values were more frequent among patients with poorer recovery at 3 months.

document_sections.heading: Interpretation
document_sections.content: At validated cutoffs, GFAP and UCH-L1 measured on a rapid automated platform accurately identified the absence of CT-detectable intracranial lesions after mTBI.

document_sections.heading: Research in context
document_sections.content: The article distinguishes the evidence available before BRAINI, the study's contribution and the possible implications of the combined evidence.

document_sections.heading: Evidence before this study
document_sections.content: Before study initiation in August 2019, S100B protein was the only biomarker incorporated into an mTBI management algorithm in some European national guidelines. GFAP and UCH-L1 had shown potential for identifying patients who might not need CT, but a rapid, dependable emergency-setting blood assay was unavailable. Their cutoff concentrations lacked external validation, and only one study had compared their combined diagnostic performance with S100B. Existing neurological-outcome models for mTBI showed only weak correlations; the relationship between injury-day biomarker concentrations and subsequent outcome required further study.

document_sections.heading: Added value of this study
document_sections.content: An automated platform measured blood GFAP and UCH-L1 within 1 h of sampling. Using cutoffs suggested by ALERT-TBI, their combined test identified patients who might not need CT in a cohort of 1438 adults with mTBI, with high sensitivity and NPV. Performance remained stable across the 12 h post-trauma sampling window. The test might outperform CCHR and NOC and lead to fewer CT prescriptions, but that comparison needs confirmation because adapted versions of those rules were assigned retrospectively. Beyond 3 h after trauma, the combined test and GFAP alone performed better than S100B for excluding the need for CT. Higher GFAP was associated with greater risk of neurological worsening. Patients with incomplete recovery or persistent symptoms at 3 months had higher blood biomarker concentrations.

document_sections.heading: Implications of all the available evidence
document_sections.content: At predetermined cutoffs, blood GFAP and UCH-L1 testing could reduce head CT use after mild TBI in adults while retaining good diagnostic performance through 12 h after trauma. Further work is needed to refine cutoffs for older people and paediatric patients and to place the test within a clinical decision algorithm.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: mTBI, defined here by an initial GCS score of 13–15, is the most common form of traumatic brain injury and affects more than 40 million people worldwide each year. Although most patients have no intracranial complication, 8–10% have an intracranial lesion, 1% require a neurosurgical procedure, and one in 1000 die. Initial assessment must identify patients at risk of complications. Head CT is the reference method for detecting acute intracranial lesions; CDRs and guidelines use patient characteristics and symptoms to inform CT decisions. Nevertheless, around 30% of prescribed scans for mTBI do not follow recommendations. S100B protein is the most extensively studied blood biomarker in this setting. The 2013 Scandinavian Guidelines included it as an option to reduce unnecessary CT among patients with mild head injury at low risk of intracranial complications or neurosurgical intervention when blood is drawn within the first 6 h; it has not been widely adopted. GFAP and UCH-L1 have complementary release kinetics after brain injury and offer a longer testing window. Their blood concentrations have been significantly higher in patients with traumatic lesions on CT than in those without lesions. Cutoffs were consequently established to predict the absence of injury on admission CT. In ALERTTBI, their combination achieved sensitivity of 97.6% and NPV of 99.6% among 1959 patients presenting within 12 h of mTBI. That study initially used a manual ELISA taking 4 h, too long for mTBI triage; its cohort was later used to validate a faster immunoassay with comparable performance. A newly developed automated assay produces results within 1 h of sampling. BRAINI aimed to validate the ALERT-TBI cutoffs externally in a multicentre European cohort. Its primary objective was to estimate combined-test sensitivity and NPV for excluding CT lesions. Secondary objectives were to compare GFAP and UCH-L1 with S100B and to compare the combined test with commonly used CDRs assigned retrospectively. The investigators also assessed neurological deterioration at 7 days and outcome at 3 months in relation to the biomarkers as potential prognostic contributors.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: BRAINI was designed to validate predefined biomarker cutoffs against independently assessed head CT findings and to examine diagnostic and neurological outcomes. The following subsections describe its design, participants, procedures, outcomes and analyses.

document_sections.heading: Study design
document_sections.content: BRAINI was a prospective, multicentre observational study in France and Spain. Recruitment ran from August 2019 through June 2021 at 16 sites: 12 in France, comprising eleven trauma centres and one community hospital, and 4 in Spain, comprising three trauma centres and one community hospital.

document_sections.heading: Ethics
document_sections.content: In Spain, CEIm Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre approved the study on 20 July 2019 (Re#19/322); the study began there on 5 August 2019. Written consent came from patients or, when they could not consent, a next of kin. In France, IRB Sud-Ouest III approved the design on 14 November 2019 (Re#2019-A01525-52), and the study began on 29 November 2019. Because the study was observational, the French committee waived written consent after information was provided and nonopposition established. Before study procedures, eligible patients or relatives received information about the objectives, sample type and volume, data collection and right to refuse participation, and had time to consider the information-and-nonopposition form. The French Data Protection Authority approved the study on 31 January 2020 (Re#919443). ClinicalTrials.gov registration NCT04032509 occurred on 25 July 2019, and the protocol was published.

document_sections.heading: Participants
document_sections.content: Eligibility required age ≥18 years in France or ≥15 years in Spain, where patients ≥15 years are managed with adults in the same emergency room by the same physician. Patients needed a post-TBI GCS score of 13–15, with TBI defined by altered brain function or other evidence of externally caused brain pathology. Routine head CT and blood sampling both had to occur within 12 h of injury. CT indications followed CCHR recommendations and other possible risks: focal neurological deficit; anterograde amnesia; GCS <15 after 2 h; suspected depressed vault fracture or basal skull fracture; persistent nausea, vomiting or headache; post-TBI seizures; preinjury antithrombotic treatment; loss of consciousness or amnesia in patients over 65 years; a fall of more than 1 m or a pedestrian being struck; or another reason judged by the treating physician to require CT. Exclusions were admission GCS 3–12; unknown injury time; unknown CT or sampling time, or either occurring more than 12 h after TBI; a nontraumatic neurological reason for admission; penetrating head injury; infeasible venipuncture; absent brain CT; judiciary control; pregnancy or breastfeeding; and participation in an ongoing interventional trial. Dementia, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, seizure disorder, brain tumor, previous neurosurgery, stroke within the last 30 days and major psychiatric disease were also exclusions because they could interfere with outcome assessment at 7 days and 3 months.

document_sections.heading: Procedures
document_sections.content: A 10-ml blood specimen was processed into serum, frozen at −80 ◦C and shipped on dry ice to central storage. Samples were allocated to three equally sized groups using site, CT assessment, GCS and age, then sent to one of three USA laboratories with the automated platform. Laboratory measurements were performed independently, blinded to clinical and CT findings. Serum GFAP and UCH-L1 were measured between September 2022 and June 2023 using VIDAS® 3 immunoassays, usually with automatic pipetting; manual pipetting was used for insufficient volume or repeat testing after an invalid result. The Analytical Measuring Interval (AMI), defined by acceptable precision and linearity, was 10.0 pg/ml to 320.0 pg/ ml for VIDAS® TBI (GFAP) and 80.0 pg/ml to 2560.0 pg/ml for VIDAS® TBI (UCH-L1). Results below the reportable range were assigned <10 pg/ml for GFAP in 142 samples and <80 pg/ml for UCH-L1 in 42 samples. Among those samples, 29 GFAP measurements were below the 5.4 pg/ ml detection limit, and one UCH-L1 measurement was below the 48.1 pg/ ml detection limit. Although individual concentrations were unavailable for these samples, their combined-test result could be classified as negative. GFAP results higher than 320 pg/ml with a signal below 6500 RFV were diluted 1/10 in negative serum and retested. Coefficients of variation for within-laboratory precision, between-lot and within-instrument measurements were below 8% for GFAP and below 7% for UCH-L1. Sample haemolysis was recorded. The combined result was positive when either biomarker reached or exceeded its cutoff—327 pg/ml for UCH-L1 or 22 pg/ml for GFAP—and negative only when both were below their cutoffs. A single blinded laboratory measured S100B protein with Elecsys® S100 on the automated Cobas® system, applying a 0.1 μg/L cutoff from the Scandinavian guidelines. In France, S100B testing required an additional information procedure; the tested subset had agreed to that analysis and provided at least three, 1 ml, serum tubes. Head CT images were assessed independently by two board-certified neuroradiologists blinded to clinical and biological findings; a third independent neuroradiologist resolved disagreements. A positive CT required one or more of these findings: epidural haematoma, acute subdural haematoma, subarachnoid haemorrhage, intraventricular haemorrhage, intraparenchymal contusion, petechial haemorrhage, or a finding related to diffuse axonal injury and depressed skull fracture. Linear skull fractures were recorded but did not constitute a positive CT. Treating physicians prospectively recorded injury mechanism, clinical features and reasons for CT. Patients were subsequently classified under retrospectively applied CCHR and NOC rules. Adaptations equated visible trauma above the clavicles with moderate or severe AIS face findings, a dangerous mechanism with a pedestrian struck by a car, and amnesia with either anterograde or retrograde amnesia; the resulting rules were termed a-CCHR and a-NOC. The physicians were in-training neurosurgeons, general practitioners and emergency medicine physicians. Retrospective rule application was chosen because most did not routinely use CDRs for CT decisions. Sex was recorded at admission as sex at birth. Data were entered into an eCRF; agreement among site data abstractors was not assessed.

document_sections.heading: Outcome measures
document_sections.content: The primary outcomes were combined GFAP–UCH-L1 sensitivity and NPV for excluding intracranial injury on head CT. Secondary diagnostic measures were specificity, PPV and the performance of GFAP, UCH-L1 and S100B protein separately. Other measures concerned neurological worsening at 7 days and altered neurological status at 3 months. Worsening at 7 days meant a GCS decline greater than 2 points from baseline or deterioration requiring osmotherapy, intensive care transfer or neurosurgical intervention. At 3 months, trained assessors blinded to clinical and biological results conducted structured telephone interviews. GOSE ranged from 1 (death) to 8 (no disability); a score <8 indicated incomplete recovery. RPQ ranged from 0 (no symptom) to 24 (severe symptoms). Under ICD criteria, PCS was considered present when at least three specified symptoms scored ≥2, indicating mild to severe problems. Those symptoms were headache, dizziness, fatigue, irritability, sleep disturbance, poor concentration, forgetfulness, poor memory, frustration and depression.

document_sections.heading: Statistics
document_sections.content: Sample-size planning used ALERT-TBI data for patients with GCS 13–15 and sought performance at least comparable to Banyan BTI. The target sensitivity of 98% had to be significantly above 93%. With a 2.5% type I error for testing H0: Sensitivity ≤93%, 80% power under H1: Sensitivity >93%, and anticipated sensitivity of at least 98%, at least 173 CT-positive patients were required. Assuming 11% CT positivity after mTBI yielded 1573 total patients, rounded to 1600; a further 10% allowance for screening failures set the recruitment target at 1760. Quantitative characteristics were reported as medians and first and third quartiles; categorical characteristics as counts and percentages. CT-positive and CT-negative groups were compared using Mann–Whitney U, Chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests, the last when expected frequencies were lower than 5. Analyses used complete observations without replacing missing values, both for the full sample and for patients with S100B measurements. Prespecified main-outcome subgroups were based on age and sex; sensitivity analyses examined GCS and time from injury to sampling. Agreement between the initial CT readers was evaluated. ROC areas and 95% confidence intervals for S100B, GFAP and UCH-L1 were estimated and compared with an algorithm suggested by DeLong. Sensitivity, specificity, NPV and PPV received 95% confidence intervals using the Agresti-Coull method. The combined test was compared with a-CCHR and a-NOC using McNemar tests for sensitivity and specificity and the generalized score statistic proposed by Leisenring for NPV and PPV. Mann–Whitney U tests compared biomarker concentrations by worsening at 7 days and outcome at 3 months. Multivariate logistic regression examined biomarker–outcome associations adjusted for age, sex and admission GCS. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05, and analyses used Stata version 17.0.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Between August 2019 and June 2021, 1508 people were assessed for BRAINI eligibility. Of these, 40 failed inclusion criteria, 27 lacked blood samples and three lacked CT results, leaving 1438 with biomarker results and valid head CT for analysis. Table 1 presents their characteristics by CT status. CT showed traumatic intracranial injury in 179 (12.4%). Positivity did not differ significantly between France and Spain: 11.1 vs 14.3%, respectively; p = 0.07. The first two CT readers had positive specific agreement of 85%, negative specific agreement of 98% and a kappa coefficient of 0.83. Compared with CT-negative patients, CT-positive patients were significantly older and more often had GCS 13 or 14, a higher median ISS score or antiplatelet treatment. Lesions included subarachnoid haemorrhage in 104 patients; 58%, acute subdural haematomas in 77 patients; 43%, intraparenchymal contusions in 36 patients; 20%, epidural haematoma in 26 patients; 14.5%, petechial haemorrhage in 10 patients; 5.6%, and intraventricular haemorrhage in 9 patients; 5%. The combined test was positive in 1121 patients (78%) and negative in 317 (22%). Negative results occurred in 38% of patients below 65 years versus 8% of older patients. Combined-test sensitivity was 98.3% (95% CI 95.0–99.7), NPV was 99.1% (95% CI 97.1–99.8), and specificity was 24.9% (95% CI 22.6–27.4). Table 2 presents diagnostic performance and the underlying test-by-CT classifications for the combined and individual biomarkers. Three patients had positive CT findings despite a negative combined test. Two had subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured nontraumatic intracranial aneurysm; the third had barely visible subarachnoid haemorrhage and no neurological deterioration during follow-up. Combined-test specificity was lower at age ≥65 years than at younger ages—10.3% (95% CI 8.2–12.8) vs 42.1% (95% CI 38.1–46.1), p < 0.001—and fell to 6.0% at age 80 and over. Sex, GCS 15 and sampling intervals of <3 h, 3–6 h or >6 h did not affect combined-test performance. Both biomarker concentrations were significantly higher with positive CT findings. For detecting CT lesions, GFAP had a greater ROC area than UCH-L1: 0.85 (95% CI 0.82–0.88) vs 0.63 (95% CI 0.58–0.67), p < 0.001.

document_sections.heading: S100B protein analysis
document_sections.content: The concomitantly tested subset comprised 1210 consenting patients with at least three, 1 ml, serum tubes. S100B protein was positive in 761, while the combined GFAP–UCH-L1 test was positive in 937. GFAP performed better diagnostically than UCH-L1 or S100B protein. Results were unchanged among patients with isolated TBI (n = 258 patients) and those with multiple extracranial injuries (n = 82 patients). During the first 3 h after trauma, S100B protein sensitivity and NPV equalled those of the combined test; beyond 3 h, they were lower. Among 98 patients sampled within the first 2 h after mTBI, biomarker diagnostic performance did not differ. For identifying intracranial injury, the ROC area was significantly greater for GFAP than for UCH-L1 or S100B protein: 0.85 (95% CI 0.82–0.88) vs 0.64 (95% CI 0.59–0.68) or 0.66 (95% CI 0.62–0.71), respectively (p < 0.001). The diagnostic-performance figure describes the 1210-patient subset and labels cutoffs of GFAP 22 pg/ml, UCH-L1 327 pg/ml and S100B 0.1 mg/ml; that last unit differs from the 0.1 μg/L S100B cutoff specified in the methods.

document_sections.heading: Clinical decision rules
document_sections.content: The combined test had higher NPV and specificity than retrospectively determined a-CCHR and a-NOC. Under a-CCHR, 1199 patients (83% of the sample) would have required CT. Among the other 239 patients (17%), whom a-CCHR would not have sent for CT, 10 had detectable lesions and a positive combined biomarker result. Applied independently of CCHR, the combined test could have avoided 317 (22%) unnecessary scans but would have missed CT abnormalities in 3 patients.

document_sections.heading: Neurological deterioration
document_sections.content: Neurological worsening related to TBI occurred in 11 patients by 7 days. Their GFAP concentrations were significantly higher than in patients without worsening: 320 pg/ml (Q1–Q3 42.5–630) vs 39.8 pg/ml (Q1–Q3 20.0–80.5), p = 0.004. No statistically significant association with worsening was demonstrated for S100B or UCH-L1. None of the patients who worsened were admitted to the ICU or underwent neurosurgical intervention.

document_sections.heading: Neurological outcomes
document_sections.content: At 3 months, GOSE information was available for 1062 (74%) patients and RPQ information for 1012 (70%). Incomplete recovery, defined by GOSE <8, affected 269 patients (25.3%); 246 patients (24.3%) had RPQ-defined PCS symptoms. Patients with altered outcomes had significantly higher admission concentrations of GFAP, UCH-L1 and S100B and more often had a positive combined test than those with complete recovery. The reported incomplete-recovery comparison was GFAP 54.9 pg/ml (Q1– Q3 27.9–145) vs 39.0 (Q1–Q3 18.2–77.6), UCH-L1 327 pg/ml (Q1–Q3 194–552) vs 248 pg/ml (Q1–Q3 160–412), and S–100 B 0.18 μg/ml (Q1–Q3 0.09–0.32) vs 0.12 μg/ml (Q1–Q3 0.07–0.20). Table 3 also presents admission concentrations by incomplete recovery and post-concussion status, with unadjusted and adjusted p-values. In age-, sex- and admission-GCS-adjusted analyses, the reported p-values for incomplete recovery were <0.001 for all three biomarkers. For persistent PCS symptoms, adjusted values were GFAP p = 0.004, UCH-L1 p = 0.001 and S100B p = 0.18; thus the reported adjusted S100B association with PCS was not statistically significant. ROC areas for incomplete recovery were 0.61, 0.60 and 0.61 for GFAP, UCH-L-1 and S100B, respectively; corresponding areas for PCS symptoms were 0.56, 0.55 and 0.57. Prognostic sensitivity was higher for GFAP and the combined GFAP-UCH-L1 test.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: At predetermined cutoffs, combined GFAP–UCH-L1 testing had high sensitivity and NPV for identifying patients without a need for CT in this European mTBI cohort. Diagnostic performance persisted across sampling times up to 12 h and across sex. Patients with altered neurological outcome at 3 months had significantly, though only marginally, higher admission concentrations. Despite CDRs and guidelines intended to guide head CT after mTBI, CT prescribing varies considerably. The Scandinavian TBI Guidelines included S100B protein for low-risk patients when used within the first 6 h, but factors including skin colour and multiple fractures have limited acceptance. GFAP and UCH-L1 emerged as candidate markers because their concentrations increase in mTBI with intracranial lesions. Earlier testing of the combined markers at predetermined cutoffs showed high sensitivity and NPV, but those cutoffs lacked external validation and any gain over GFAP alone remained uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic performance with the automated immunoassay
document_sections.content: The automated assay was designed to provide GFAP and UCH-L1 results less than 1 h after blood sampling, making testing practicable in emergency care. The authors compare this turnaround with guidance that, when indicated for intermediate- and medium-risk patients, CT should occur within 8 h of trauma. BRAINI confirmed that the ALERT-TBI cutoffs—GFAP 22 pg/ml and UCH-L1 327 pg/ml—could exclude CT-detectable intracranial injury after mTBI. The combined test outperformed S100B when sampling took place after 3 h, which applied to 75% of this population, and the authors consider its wider postinjury sampling window consistent with other studies. Recent French National Recommendations suggested S100B within the first 3 h or, if available, combined GFAP–UCH-L1 within 12 h. The authors describe BRAINI as, to their knowledge, the largest direct comparison of two clinically available European brain-biomarker approaches. GFAP alone had the greatest sensitivity and NPV; unlike ALERT-TBI, BRAINI did not confirm that adding UCH-L1 improved GFAP performance. The authors suggest older age or longer injury-to-sampling time as possible explanations. Of three false-negative patients, two fell because of a ruptured intracerebral aneurysm. The authors call for research on biomarker performance in nontraumatic conditions, including intracerebral haematoma and subarachnoid haemorrhage. The third had minimal traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage without deterioration; all three would have undergone CT under CCHR. Specificity and the proportion of negative tests decreased above age 65 years, with a further specificity reduction among octogenarians. Prior studies have reported correlations of S100, GFAP, UCH-L1 and NF-L concentrations with age and neurological or neurodegenerative conditions. The authors therefore suggest revising cutoffs for older patients, as planned in the ongoing BRAINI2 elderly study.

document_sections.heading: Biomarkers and CDRs
document_sections.content: The study's data suggest that the combined test could surpass CCHR and NOC for predicting CT findings, but its CDR comparisons used adapted rules applied retrospectively. Biomarkers seek to capture nearly any posttraumatic CT abnormality to maximize sensitivity, whereas CDRs seek to avoid missing neurosurgical and clinically important lesions while maintaining reasonable specificity, potentially missing small lesions without clinical significance. Other studies have suggested that CCHR combined with GFAP might provide the highest accuracy for predicting CT abnormalities in adult mTBI, but those studies either did not report GFAP cutoffs or did not specify how to combine the two. A study by Papa et al. is described as supporting joint assessment of biomarkers and CDRs with clinical rule factors recorded prospectively by treating physicians; the authors consider such an approach potentially optimal. BRAINI did not establish where biomarkers belong in an mTBI management algorithm because CT decisions were independent of biomarker results. The authors call for definition of the target population and an algorithm incorporating clinical and blood-biomarker information. Ongoing studies NCT05885529 in France and NCT06449183 in the USA may add evidence about combined use and real-world performance.

document_sections.heading: Biomarkers and neurological outcome
document_sections.content: Most patients with mTBI can resume normal life, but some experience persistent symptoms affecting work and social life. Absence of a CT-visible lesion does not ensure absence of persistent post-TBI symptoms. The strongest mTBI prognostic models use symptoms and outcomes assessed one week after injury; accordingly, outcome cannot currently be predicted in the emergency setting. The TRACK and CENTER-TBI studies have contributed to interest in S100B, GFAP and UCH-L1 as prognostic blood markers. In BRAINI, admission median GFAP and UCH-L1 concentrations were significantly higher among patients later showing incomplete recovery or persistent PCS-related symptoms. After covariate adjustment, each biomarker was associated with incomplete recovery, although concentration differences were marginal. If confirmed, these findings could support biomarker-inclusive models for identifying patients at risk of incomplete recovery.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: BRAINI validated an automated assay rather than testing clinical implementation: CT was prescribed without regard to biomarker findings, so real-world use of the tests for CT triage still needs evaluation. CT indications also differed among countries, centres and physicians because of prescriber- and patient-related factors. The intracranial-lesion frequency was high (12%), which the authors say may indicate physician use of CDRs and an absence of indiscriminate CT scanning. The higher-than-expected frequency of CT positivity prevented a potential loss of power for the primary endpoint despite the smaller sample. Although frequent CT positivity was expected to disadvantage NPV estimates, observed NPV met the prespecified expectation. Alternative biomarker cutoffs were not examined because validation of earlier cutoffs was the objective. Decision-rule accuracy was derived from an automated application to recorded risk factors rather than physician judgement, using adapted rules constrained by eCRF data; this may have affected CDR performance and differs from studies in which emergency physicians completed rule forms prospectively before CT. The CDR comparison therefore requires caution. The study was neither designed nor powered to formally evaluate the three secondary areas comprising CDR comparisons, neurological deterioration at 7 days and outcome at 3 months. Participants were relatively old, and falls predominated. Although their age profile reflects European emergency admissions, results may not generalize to younger emergency populations with different injury mechanisms, such as those in North America. The authors add that TBI in older people is increasing worldwide, so similar patient populations may become more common. Despite significant biomarker differences by neurological status at 3 months, their magnitude was small; these results need caution and further study. Finally, logistical constraints across participating sites prevented collection of the total number of potentially screened patients.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that automated blood testing could provide an objective way to screen patients with mTBI and identify those who do not need brain CT in less than 1 h. They consider the studied cutoffs potentially useful for safe, accurate acute-care triage across countries. Combined GFAP–UCH-L1 testing might discriminate better than S100B protein beyond 3 h after trauma.
